A pilot who organised a survey of nearly 300 two-liner owners treats under about 20 hours on your previous wing as a warning sign before a two-liner specifically — and has a real case attached: someone who moved onto one with around 11 hours, took a severe collapse in rough terrain, and threw their reserve. gates.message: This is the one skill two experts who disagree about almost everything else agree matters before a two-liner. Fewer lines give collapsing fabric more room to tangle, so cravats are more likely here than on the wing you're on, and clearing one isn't the same instinct as clearing an ordinary collapse. Practised, deliberately, over water or with a coach, is what this needs.

gates.message: This is the other skill both experts agree on, whatever they disagree about elsewhere. A two-liner hands you pitch movement sooner and wants a lighter touch than the wing you're on — catching a surge on the brakes, holding it on the rear risers while you're on bar, easing off before it dives. Worth building deliberately rather than meeting for the first time on the new wing.

gates.message: Managing the energy that comes out of a frontal collapse is on the short list of things one detailed analysis expects before a two-liner. gates.message: In a survey of nearly 300 pilots flying two-line C wings, about a quarter had real difficulty getting ears in on the shorter line set — and the survey names it as one of its specific warning signs. gates.message: The same survey names leaning on the bar passively, without working the brakes as the wing accelerates, as a specific warning sign — it gives a feeling of security rather than actual control, on exactly the wings where that control matters most. Easing the bar on while watching the pitch, and trimming the pressure as you go, is the habit worth building first.

No question asks whether the pilot skipped a rung, and no scoring path treats it differently either way — see meta.design_decisions 'v1-loidl-counter-example-stays-informational'.

gate_behaviour.rule: Any fired gate caps the recommendation at Not yet, regardless of score.
gate_behaviour.evaluation_order: Gates are evaluated first and short-circuit: if any gate fires, the recommendation is Not yet and the threshold rules are not evaluated.
gate_behaviour.tone_rule: Gate messages state what to work on and why, never that the pilot is unsuitable. No message may imply EN-D is a uniform class — the Enzo/Zeno variation is real and named in suggestions, not glossed over.

source.cites: Hard gates cap the result regardless of total score.
source.note: 17 gates total (10 universal + 6 two-liner-conditional + 1 new currency gate counted among the universal set), matching low-c-to-high-c's count with one added and none removed.

rule_messages.purpose: Pilot-safe copy for the threshold rules, same pattern as every reviewed step so far.

algorithm: 3. if still not found: render nothing for that rule.
lookup.multiplicity: critical_check_floor breaks on its first failing question (order matters, see thresholds.ready.critical_check_floor.source). Gates and rules are mutually exclusive.

critical_check_floor:airtime_last_12m.message: One thing is holding this back: how much you've flown this year. This is the single best-evidenced figure in the whole research for this step — two separate industry sources converge closely on 100-plus hours a year, ongoing. You're not quite there yet. More time in the air this year, on the wing you already trust, is what moves this.

source.cites: The 100+/year consensus.
source.note: Reached by the 25_50 or 50_100 bands; under_25 is a hard gate.

critical_check_floor:current_wing_time.message: One thing is holding this back: time on the wing you're on now. More time on the wing you already trust, flown properly rather than just logged, is what moves this.

source.cites: Lindenstruth's survey.
source.note: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:collapse_practice.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the one place this step genuinely asks more of you than the wing you're on does. The certification wording for this class describes demanding handling needing precise, immediate input to recover. Wingovers, a controlled spiral, a bigger asymmetric with someone watching — the suggestion below has the order to do it in.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:pitch_control.message: One thing is holding this back: damping a surge or a dive when the wing moves on you. Catching it on the brakes, then holding it on the rear risers while you're on bar, is the progression worth practising.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:cravat_recovery.message: One thing is holding this back: clearing a cravat. Never having had one isn't the problem by itself — not having practised clearing one deliberately is. A session over water with a coach is the direct fix.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:wing_limiting_evide.message: One thing is holding this back: by your own account, your current wing hasn't clearly been the thing stopping you yet. That usually means there's performance still sitting in it, which is worth collecting first.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:active_piloting.message: One thing is holding this back: what your hands do when the air gets bumpy. This class needs genuinely active, continuous input, unlike wings that mostly recover on their own. Light, friendly bumps are the place to build the habit, not the big days.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:thermal_turn_contro.message: One thing is holding this back: thermalling that works but isn't yet fully under your control. The suggestion below has specific things to drill.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:response_when_rough.message: One thing is holding this back, and it isn't nerves — that part is normal. It's what happens next: tightening up and waiting it out rather than carrying on flying the wing. That builds like any other habit.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:flying_frequency.message: One thing is holding this back: how often you're actually getting in the air right now, over the last three months specifically. Two or three times a month changes this and several other answers with it.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:collapse_experience.message: One thing is holding this back, and it isn't that you froze — that's the normal starting point, not a character flaw. It's that the reaction hasn't been tested yet. It's trainable, and the wing you're on is a better one to learn on than the one you're shopping for.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:reserve_familiarity.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the quickest to fix: not being certain you could find the reserve handle in a hurry. Two minutes in a hang check changes this permanently.

source.cites: Carried forward.

unevidenced_core_checks:thermal_turn_con.message: One thing is unevidenced rather than weak. You've said thermalling mostly hasn't come up, so it scores as neutral, not against you. But there isn't a reading of the guidance for this step that a soaring-only pilot clears — this is an XC and competition-oriented class by every source that discusses it. Worth knowing plainly rather than finding out later.

source.cites: Carried forward.

ready_category_floor:skills.message: Your total is in the ready band, but the skills and experience half isn't carrying its own weight yet. The suggestions below are the specific parts of it.

source.cites: Carried forward.

ready_category_floor:psychological.message: Your total is in the ready band, but the mindset and motivation half is sitting well below the skills half. At this step they count for nearly as much as each other.

source.cites: Carried forward.

not_yet_category_floor:skills.message: The skills and experience answers point the same way: more flying and more deliberate practice on the wing you've got, not a different wing. Every one of the things that moves this transfers to whatever you fly next.

source.cites: Carried forward.

not_yet_category_floor:psychological.message: This one isn't about your hands. Why the change, what you expect it to give you, and how decisions get made on a day you're unsure about are where this result comes from — and none of that is a judgement on you as a pilot. It usually takes a conversation rather than another fifty hours in the air.

source.cites: Carried forward.
source.note: The more serious of the two floors.

conservative_backstop.message: A few of the main questions were left blank, so there isn't quite enough here to put the result any higher than this. Nothing is counted against you for skipping them — filling them in is the whole fix.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor.message: One specific check for this step came out low, and a single weak answer holds the result here even when everything else is strong. The suggestions below name which one and what moves it.

unevidenced_core_checks.message: One of the checks for this step hasn't been tested rather than failed. That isn't counted against you, but the result stays here until there's something to go on.

ready_category_floor.message: Your total is in the ready band, but one half of it is sitting well below the other. They're scored separately on purpose.

not_yet_category_floor.message: One of the two halves of this came out low enough to decide the result on its own. That's a normal, useful result — it means there's a specific half to work on.

always_output.instructor_recommendation: Whatever this says, run it past an instructor or coach who has seen you fly — and test-fly the specific wing before you buy it. That matters more here than anywhere else on the ladder: EN-D covers everything from an XC-oriented open wing to a pure competition wing, and someone who knows both you and the specific wing is doing work no form can do.
always_output.disclaimer: This is a self-assessment tool based on published guidance from national associations, manufacturers, retailers and instructors. It isn't an instructor, it can't see you fly, and it isn't a safety clearance. Wing choice is your responsibility and your instructor's advice always comes first.
always_output.methodology_note: This is the step the research treats as needing the clearest extra caution. The one figure almost everyone agrees on is annual currency — 100-plus hours a year, kept up, not banked once — and it carries real weight here because it's genuinely well corroborated, not because the app has decided to be strict for its own sake. Everything else leans on a smaller set of expert and manufacturer voices, which is close to unavoidable at a level only a small share of pilots ever reach — treat that material as serious judgement, not as a settled standard the way the hours figure is. Every weight and gate links back to the criterion it came from.

source.cites: A recommendation to discuss the upgrade with an instructor, plus a clear disclaimer.
